rationale: Start with a broad gradient to observe all six compounds and locate critical pairs, while targeting an elution window near 10 minutes. The high final organic fraction reduces the risk of retained compounds remaining unobserved.
The first method already achieves the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient to test for faster elution while preserving full resolution, keeping the original method as the established optimum.
Shorten the gradient by one grid step to reduce elution time while testing whether the earliest pair retains R ≥ 1.5. The 6-minute gradient remains a fully resolved fallback with maximum CRF.
Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed limit at 40 °C; the earliest pair may drop below R = 1.5. If it does, the 4-minute gradient is the fully resolved, maximum-CRF fallback.

Return to the shortest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature one experimental increment to seek faster elution. This also tests how temperature affects the critical early pair before attempting further acceleration.
Back off temperature by one grid step to test the boundary between faster elution and full resolution of the early pair. The 40 °C method remains the shortest confirmed method achieving CRF 1.000.

Raise the starting organic fraction to seek earlier elution while retaining the successful 4-minute gradient and 40 °C temperature. This tests whether narrowing the gradient window preserves full resolution of the critical early pair.
Further narrow the gradient window by raising the starting organic fraction, seeking faster elution at the same maximum CRF. Monitor the early pair for loss of retention and resolution.

Back off the starting organic fraction by one grid step to locate the fastest fully resolved method between the successful 0.20 and unsuccessful 0.30 starts. This preserves the established gradient duration and temperature.

Test whether cooling restores early-pair selectivity enough to permit a 2-minute gradient, using the starting fraction that gave the strongest early-pair resolution at 4 minutes. The 0.25–0.95, 4-minute, 40 °C method remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.

Raise the starting organic fraction by one grid step to seek faster elution with the successful 2-minute, 25 °C gradient. The early pair has little resolution margin, so this tests the boundary while retaining injection 10 as a maximum-CRF fallback.

Increase the starting organic fraction by one more grid step, since the previous increase improved early-pair resolution while shortening elution. Test whether that trend continues without sacrificing the maximum CRF.

Use the improved early-pair resolution margin to test a one-step temperature increase for faster elution. Keep the minimum gradient duration and starting fraction fixed to isolate the temperature response.

Test a higher starting organic fraction at the temperature that provides more early-pair selectivity. This explores whether further narrowing the gradient can shorten elution while maintaining full resolution; injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Return to the successful 0.30 starting fraction and test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method. This establishes whether further acceleration is possible before the early pair falls below R = 1.5.

Back off to the successful temperature and lower final organic fraction one step to test a gentler gradient with greater early-pair resolution margin. CRF is already maximized; this explores a lower-organic alternative to the fastest confirmed method without repeating an injection.

Lower the starting fraction one step to assess the early-pair resolution boundary around the successful reduced-organic method. Injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, and the maximum CRF is already secured.

Raise the final organic fraction one step from injection 17 to shorten late-peak elution and test whether the early pair remains fully resolved. This completes a local comparison around injection 13, the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Test a gentler gradient at the temperature with stronger early-pair selectivity to obtain more resolution margin while keeping elution near 3 minutes. Injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; the maximum CRF is already secured.

Lower the final organic fraction one more grid step to test whether a gentler gradient increases the critical pair’s resolution margin while retaining CRF 1.000. Injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Raise temperature one grid step to shorten elution for the reduced-organic method, using its additional early-pair resolution margin. The campaign has already achieved maximum CRF, with injection 13 still the fastest confirmed fully resolved option.

Test whether a lower starting fraction and gentler slope preserve early-pair resolution at 35 °C, where the steeper gradient failed. This explores a warmer, fully resolved alternative while retaining injection 13 as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Back off temperature one grid step from injection 22 to recover full early-pair resolution with the reduced-organic gradient. Injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed method achieving the maximum CRF of 1.000.

Test the remaining nearby combination expected to provide more early-pair resolution margin than injection 17 while keeping elution below 3 minutes. Injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, and the maximum CRF is already secured.

Use the final injection to test a nearby gentler gradient expected to retain maximum CRF with additional early-pair resolution margin. Injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method: 0.30–0.95 organic over 2 minutes at 30 °C, with the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
